title: In Hungary in 1946, prices doubled roughly every 15 hours
body: After the Second World War, Hungary suffered the worst hyperinflation on record. At its peak, in July 1946, it took about 15 hours for prices to double. The central bank issued a 100 quintillion pengő note, its largest ever, before replacing the pengő with the forint in August 1946.

slides.prompt: What was the face value of the biggest banknote Hungary issued?
slides.detail: Issued on 11 July 1946. Notes for ten times as much were printed but never issued, and the forint replaced the pengő in August 1946.

slides.alt: Animated engraved banknote: a 24-hour clock runs while a price tag doubles every 15 hours, from 1 to 65,536 pengő in ten days. A 100 quintillion pengő note runs out of room, a dollar's black-market price grows to 31 digits, and 1 forint replaces 400 octillion pengő.
slides.music: “Magic Escape Room” Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com) · CC BY 4.0

slides.heading: How many days prices took to double, at each hyperinflation’s peak
slides.note: Hours for Hungary (14.82) and Zimbabwe (24.35) turned into days; Wikipedia’s 2012 table
slides.explanation: Hungary’s prices doubled every 15 hours and Zimbabwe’s about every day. Germany’s famous 1923 inflation was far slower at its peak: 3.65 days.

slides.clue: The currency that replaced the pengő in August 1946, and is still Hungary’s money today
slides.detail: Named after Florence, whose gold florins were minted from 1252; Hungary struck its own gold florentinus from 1325 under Charles Robert.
